title: Advanced features — MERGE, OUTPUT, JSON, dynamic SQL, stored procedures
exp: MERGE (upsert), OUTPUT (capture changes), and JSON functions are real-world T-SQL features that appear in senior SQL interviews and the kind of compliance/integration work you're already doing. Dynamic SQL is asked for its risks and safe patterns.
pts: **MERGE:** combines INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE into a single statement based on a match condition — classic upsert pattern. Use carefully: known edge cases with duplicate matches in source.
**OUTPUT clause:** captures the rows affected by INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE into a result set or table variable — useful for audit trails, returning IDs of inserted rows, or capturing before/after values

**JSON in SQL Server:** `FOR JSON PATH` / `FOR JSON AUTO` — serialize query results to JSON; `JSON_VALUE(col, '$.key')` — extract a scalar; `JSON_QUERY(col, '$.array')` — extract an object/array; `OPENJSON(col)` — parse JSON into rows
**Dynamic SQL:** build and execute SQL strings at runtime using `sp_executesql @sql, @params, @val`; use parameterised queries to prevent SQL injection
**SQL injection risk:** NEVER concatenate user input directly into a SQL string. Use sp_executesql with typed parameters.
Stored procedures: compiled, can have input/output parameters, support transactions, reduce network round-trips; trade-off: business logic in DB vs application layer
Temp tables (#) in stored procedures reset on each execution; table variables (@) go out of scope at end of batch
pr: Write a MERGE for a SCIM user sync (insert if new, update if changed, deactivate if removed)

viz.note: Practice writing a MERGE statement for your SCIM provisioning scenario — this directly maps to your production work.

qa.q: What is the MERGE statement and what is its main gotcha?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** MERGE combines INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE into a single statement based on a match condition between a target table and a source. It's the SQL upsert operator. The main gotcha: if the source has duplicate rows matching the same target row, the MERGE raises an error. Always de-duplicate the source first: WITH deduped AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM source) ... SELECT * FROM deduped WHERE rn = 1.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: What does the OUTPUT clause do and give two practical use cases?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** OUTPUT captures the rows affected by a data modification (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and returns them as a result set or inserts them into a table. Use case 1: get the auto-generated IDs after a bulk INSERT without a separate SELECT. Use case 2: audit trail — UPDATE employees SET salary = salary*1.1 OUTPUT DELETED.salary AS before, INSERTED.salary AS after INTO salary_audit — captures before and after values in a single statement.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Sync-over-async (.Result or .Wait()) on ASP.NET request threads rapidly exhausts thread pool threads, leading to HTTP 503 gateway timeouts and request queuing under load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.

qa.q: What are the JSON functions in SQL Server and when do you use each?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** FOR JSON PATH/AUTO: serialize query results to a JSON string — use when your API or client expects JSON. JSON_VALUE(col, '$.key'): extract a single scalar value from a JSON column — use for filtering or selecting individual fields. JSON_QUERY(col, '$.nested'): extract a JSON object or array (not a scalar) — preserves JSON structure. OPENJSON(col): parse a JSON string into a table of rows — use when you receive JSON documents and need to query them relationally. ISJSON(col): validate whether a string is valid JSON.

qa.q: What is SQL injection and how does sp_executesql prevent it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** SQL injection is when user-supplied input is concatenated into a SQL string and executed as code. If a user inputs '; DROP TABLE users; -- as a parameter, string concatenation executes the DROP. sp_executesql with parameters prevents this: the parameter value is passed separately and treated as data, never as SQL code, regardless of its content. Always use sp_executesql @sql, @params_definition, @param = @value pattern for dynamic SQL with user input.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** EF Core builds an Expression Tree, translates it via the relational SQL provider into a parameterized T-SQL query, and materializes entities into the DbContext Change Tracker. N+1 queries occur when navigating un-included navigation properties in a loop.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing queries without AsNoTracking() in read-only APIs forces EF Core to keep snapshot copies of all returned entities in memory, causing high RAM usage and CPU tracking overhead.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** AsNoTracking() speeds up read queries by 20-30% and reduces memory footprint, but disables identity resolution and automatic change tracking for updates.

qa.q: What are the trade-offs of putting business logic in stored procedures vs the application layer?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Stored procedures: compiled execution plan, reduced network round-trips, enforced schema, centralised logic. Trade-offs: harder to version control and test, tightly coupled to the database, requires DBA permissions for changes. Application layer: easier to test, version control, and deploy independently; uses familiar .NET/ORM patterns; but requires more network round-trips and loses SQL Server compilation benefits. Most modern teams prefer application-layer logic (using EF Core or Dapper) and reserve stored procedures for performance-critical or DBA-managed operations.
